title: Weather and the four seasons
goal: Talk about the weather, get to know Iran's four distinct seasons, and understand the calendar that shapes Iranian life.
bekal: ask and answer what the weather is like
use weather verbs that have no dummy subject
recognize four holidays that bring all of Iran to a stop

dialogs.title: گفتگو — زمستانِ تهران
dialogs.intro: Early December. Budi is shivering at a bus stop, and Maryam finds him in a jacket that's far too thin.

lines.baca: salâm! cherâ inghadr kam-lebâs? havâ kheyli sard ast.
lines.id: Hi! Why are you dressed so lightly? It's really cold.
lines.literal: hello! why this-much little-clothes? air very cold is.

lines.text: در کشورِ ما زمستان نداریم. من به سرما عادت ندارم.
lines.baca: dar keshvar-e mâ zemestân nadârim. man be sarmâ âdat nadâram.

notes: ⚠️ **Persian weather verbs have no dummy subject.** باران می‌آید literally means "rain comes" — the rain itself is the subject. برف می‌آید = "snow comes". English forces in an *it* that refers to nothing (*it rains*); Persian doesn't.

**"I'm not used to it" = عادت ندارم.** The word عادت ("habit") is an Arabic loanword you'll meet in many languages. به چیزی عادت داشتن = "to be used to something", به چیزی عادت کردن = "to get used to something".
**"I can't believe it" = باورم نمی‌شود**, literally "my belief doesn't happen". A set phrase for surprise. Its relatives: عجب! ("wow!"), واقعاً؟ ("really?"), نه بابا! ("no way!").

⚠️ **Iran has four real seasons, and that surprises many visitors.** Tehran's winter drops below zero with snow in the streets; Yazd's summer passes fifty degrees. This isn't a desert that's hot all year — it's a high mountain country with three different climates inside one border. If you visit, check which month and which city; your jacket depends on it.

**"Come on, let's" = بیایید.** The invitation form of آمدن. Used just like English "let's": بیایید برویم ("let's go"), بیایید بخوریم ("let's eat"). The verb form after it is the التزامی, covered fully in unit 18.
**Spoken forms:** هوا چطوره؟ (*havâ chetowre?*), خیلی سرده (*kheyli sarde*), برف میاد (*barf miyâd*), بارون میاد (*bârun miyâd* — note باران → بارون).

grammars.title: Talking about the weather
after: Notice the ending **ـی** at work again, making weather adjectives: آفتاب ("sun") → آفتابی، ابر ("cloud") → ابری، باران → بارانی، برف → برفی، باد → بادی.

Weather forecasts use a form you haven't learned yet, but the sentences are fixed and easy to memorize: فردا باران می‌آید ("it will rain tomorrow"), فردا هوا بهتر می‌شود ("the weather will improve tomorrow").

grammars.title: Four seasons and twelve months
after: ⚠️ **The Iranian year starts on the first day of spring**, around March 20–21. So the first month (فروردین) falls in late March, not January, and Iranian dates always run about three months "behind" what you're used to.

For Western calendar months, Iranians use the French names: ژانویه (*zhânviye*), فوریه، مارس، آوریل، مه، ژوئن، ژوئیه، اوت، سپتامبر، اکتبر، نوامبر، دسامبر. You'll see them on flights, in international mail, and in foreign news.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Nowruz (نوروز) is the most important thing to know before planning a trip.** For about two weeks in late March, all of Iran stops: offices close, schools are out, and the whole population travels at once. Tickets sell out, hotels are full, and any official business is impossible. If you're coming as a tourist, it's a beautiful time; if you're coming to work, avoid it.

blocks.title: Yalda night (شبِ یلدا), celebrated since before Islam
items: The longest night of the year (the winter solstice) is celebrated by Iranian families staying up together all night: watermelon and pomegranates red as the dawn, nuts, and readings of Hafez's poetry to tell the coming year's fortune (فالِ حافظ).

The name یلدا itself comes from Syriac and means "birth" — the night the sun is born again. It's one of the celebrations that has run unbroken since Zoroastrian times, and one of the best reasons to be in Iran in December.

blocks.title: Iran's dress code, short and honest
items: **Women** — in public, hair must be covered (روسری or شال) and loose clothing must cover the hips to the thighs (مانتو). Trousers are fine; long skirts too. The rules apply to foreigners and Iranians alike.
**Men** — trousers and short sleeves are fine; shorts aren't worn in public except at men's beaches and sports grounds.

Inside someone's home, among family and close guests, all those rules come off. What applies is public etiquette, not private etiquette — and you'll feel the difference the moment you step into your first Iranian home.
